children: HUMP DAY DATA: THE SECRET WORD IS...
It's "affordability," of course, with data on mortgages and consumer credit on the docket.
Starting with the former, financing home loans grew more expensive last week, and potential borrowers were having none of it.
The average 30-year fixed contract rate—which generally tracks the benchmark U.S. Treasury yield—increased by 6 basis points to 6.85%, the highest it's been since June 2025.

That jump didn't really put much of a dent in demand for loans to purchase homes, which inched a negligible 0.2% lower. Refi applications, on the other hand—which accounted for a decreasing 40.9% share of the mortgage pie—tanked 6.2%.
Combined, home loan demand slid by 2.7% last week.

"Mortgage rates moved higher last week, driven by ongoing investor concerns over inflation and the federal budget deficit,” writes Joel Kan, MBA’s deputy chief economist. "Refinance applications remain significantly impacted by these higher rates, falling to the slowest weekly pace since May 2025."
"Higher mortgage rates continue to weigh on prospective homebuyers looking to act, even as housing inventory has increased in many markets," Kan adds.
The 30-year fixed rate has been above 6% for more than four years now, and has been blamed by homebuilders and realtors for the affordability crisis weighing on the sector.
The rate now sits 36 basis points above where it was during the same week a year ago.
Over that same period, purchase applications have decreased by 6.9%, while refi demand has plunged by 32.1% in the last 12 months.
Pivoting to the consumer, who shoulders about 70% of the U.S. economy, late Tuesday afternoon the Federal Reserve released its latest report on consumer credit outstanding.
The report showed that consumer debt unexpectedly surged by $18.06 billion in July, a 24% acceleration from the previous month.
That's $6.4 billion north of consensus.
Peeking under the hood, non-revolving credit—which includes big-ticket items like tuition and automobiles—grew by $15.5 billion, nearly double the prior month's $7.8 billion increase.
But revolving credit, which includes credit card debt, decelerated by 58.3%, increasing by $2.8 billion, versus June's 6.7% gain.
On monthly annualized bases, revolving and non-revolving credit outstanding have grown 2.5% and 4.8%, respectively.

There's been growing chatter about the K-shaped economy, in which wealthier Americans (i.e., stockholders) are enjoying boom times, while consumers at the lower end of the scale are suffering a cost-of-living squeeze.
But the recent uptick in the saving rate, sour consumer survey readings, and this deceleration of credit card spending all point to an increasing reluctance to spend.
